paragraphs: A language model learning to use tools can learn from both successful decisions and unsuccessful explorations. This paper examines a training approach that previously kept only successful routes through a tree of tool-use decisions. Discarding the failed branches leaves potentially useful evidence about which decisions the model should avoid.

The proposed framework turns these branching expert trajectories into preferences between individual steps. Training then proceeds in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on successful tool-use trajectories, followed by direct preference optimization using the constructed preferences. The resulting model, TP-LLaMA, therefore learns from successful demonstrations and from comparisons informed by errors already present in the original data.

The experiments report substantial improvements over the baselines in almost all tested scenarios, better generalization to unseen APIs, and greater reasoning efficiency. These findings support the value of extracting additional supervision from existing search histories. The contribution is a way to make failed exploration useful during training, rather than treating a successful final trajectory as the only informative part of an expert's reasoning process.
neurips-2024-advancing-tool-augmented-la.tldr: TP-LLaMA learns preferences from failed and successful tool-use explorations, improving performance, generalization, and reasoning efficiency in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: BABILong evaluates whether language models can reason using facts scattered through very long documents. A large input capacity alone does not establish that a model can connect relevant information within it. The benchmark makes this distinction concrete through 20 tasks involving operations such as chaining facts, deduction, induction, counting, and working with lists or sets.

The necessary facts appear amid long stretches of natural text, combining the challenge of finding information with the challenge of reasoning over it. In the reported evaluations, popular language models effectively use only 10–20% of their context, and performance drops sharply as reasoning becomes more complex. Tested retrieval-augmented approaches achieve about 60% accuracy on single-fact questions, independently of context length.

Among the evaluated context-extension methods, fine-tuned recurrent memory transformers perform best and process sequences reaching 50 million tokens. The released benchmark splits extend to 10 million tokens, while the construction can support arbitrary lengths. The results distinguish nominal context capacity from demonstrated reasoning ability and provide a framework for testing both as models develop.
neurips-2024-babilong-testing-the-limits.tldr: BABILong tests reasoning over facts scattered through long documents and reveals substantial gaps between context capacity and effective use.

paragraphs: Smoke segmentation identifies which image pixels belong to smoke, supporting applications such as fire response and gas-leak detection. Producing reliable training labels is difficult because smoke has blurry boundaries, diverse appearances, and varying transparency. These properties also mean that incorrectly labeled examples can have inconsistent visual features, complicating efforts to reduce their influence during training.

CoSW addresses this problem by making sample weighting conditional on feature clusters. It uses multiple prototypes as reference information, allowing different clusters to follow different weighting criteria. Instead of applying one shared rule across all appearances, the method uses the prototype structure to guide how training samples contribute to learning.

The paper also introduces regularized within-prototype entropy to implement the weighting approach and keep prototype updates stable. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on both real-world and synthetic datasets with noisy smoke labels. The findings support adapting noise-handling rules to the different visual patterns within smoke data, with the prototype framework connecting those patterns to the training process.
neurips-2024-cosw-conditional-sample-wei.tldr: CoSW uses prototype-dependent sample weighting to improve smoke segmentation when pixel labels are noisy.

paragraphs: Long-range time-series forecasting can benefit from stable patterns that repeat over time. CycleNet explicitly represents these recurring patterns instead of leaving their discovery entirely to a forecasting network. The approach separates the repeating component of a sequence from the remaining variation, giving the prediction model a more focused task.

Its central technique, Residual Cycle Forecasting, learns recurrent cycles that describe the sequence's periodic structure. It then predicts the residual component left after accounting for those cycles. Combining this technique with either a linear layer or a shallow multilayer perceptron produces CycleNet. The design makes explicit periodic modeling compatible with a small, relatively simple forecasting model.

The paper reports state-of-the-art accuracy across domains including electricity, weather, and energy, together with a reduction of more than 90% in the required parameter count. Residual Cycle Forecasting also improves existing models, including PatchTST and iTransformer, when added as a separate component. These findings suggest that explicitly modeling stable recurrence can improve both compact predictors and more elaborate forecasting architectures.
neurips-2024-cyclenet-enhancing-time-ser.tldr: CycleNet learns repeating time-series patterns and forecasts their residuals, achieving strong reported accuracy with substantially fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Motion forecasting for autonomous driving must represent several plausible futures while also describing how a traffic participant's state changes over time. Many approaches assign one internal query to each complete possible trajectory. DeMo addresses the concern that this representation may not capture enough detail about a trajectory's evolving states.

The framework separates trajectory queries into two groups. Mode queries describe distinct directional intentions, while state queries represent dynamic states over time. This separation lets the model optimize the diversity of possible movements and their temporal evolution individually. It then combines the two query types to construct a more detailed representation of each predicted trajectory.

DeMo uses attention for aggregating global information and Mamba techniques for modeling state sequences. These components support the two complementary parts of its trajectory representation. Experiments on Argoverse 2 and nuScenes report state-of-the-art forecasting performance. The results support the paper's central design choice: giving directional alternatives and evolving motion states explicit, separate representations before integrating them into predictions.
neurips-2024-demo-decoupling-motion-fore.tldr: DeMo separates directional intentions from evolving motion states to improve forecasts of multiple possible traffic trajectories.

paragraphs: Depth-wise separable convolutions provide useful representations with relatively few parameters and computations. Their existing compactness makes further pruning difficult, especially for the depth-wise component. DEPrune tackles this problem by considering how these operations actually execute on GPUs, connecting the choice of what to remove with the hardware's ability to accelerate the remaining work.

The method prunes both point-wise and depth-wise convolutions. Although it makes fine-grained pruning decisions, it produces structured sparsity that supports practical hardware acceleration. This combination matters because the arrangement of the remaining computation determines whether pruning translates into faster execution. The paper also introduces balanced workload tuning and hardware-aware sparsity recalibration to improve performance further.

The reported experiments achieve up to a 3.74-fold practical speedup for depth-wise separable convolution inference on GPUs while preserving EfficientNet-B0 accuracy on ImageNet. This is an empirical result for the evaluated setting, with the maximum speedup qualified as 'up to.' The work demonstrates how pruning designed around GPU computation can make an already compact convolutional model faster.
neurips-2024-deprune-depth-wise-separabl.tldr: DEPrune structures fine-grained convolution pruning for GPU execution, reporting up to 3.74-fold speedup while preserving the evaluated model's accuracy.

paragraphs: Egocentric computer vision has largely concentrated on cameras worn on the head. EgoSim explores cameras placed across the body, which can provide additional perspectives for motion tracking, pose estimation, and activity recognition. These viewpoints are particularly relevant to the lower body, which is often hidden from existing views.

The simulator generates realistic images from multiple body-mounted camera positions and uses real motion-capture data to reproduce motion artifacts. Those artifacts are especially noticeable for cameras attached to arms or legs. Its accompanying MultiEgoView dataset contains six-camera footage with full-body 3D pose references: 119 hours generated from AMASS motion sequences in four virtual environments, plus five hours of real recordings from 13 participants.

The real recordings use six GoPro cameras and an Xsens motion-capture suit for pose references. To evaluate usefulness, the authors train an end-to-end network that estimates 3D body pose from video alone. Their analysis of the simulation-to-reality gap finds that the simulator and dataset substantially help training for real-world inference, supporting body-wide camera simulation as a useful source of training data.
neurips-2024-egosim-an-egocentric-multi-.tldr: EgoSim and MultiEgoView provide simulated and real body-camera footage that helps train video-based 3D pose estimation for real-world use.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models can generate high-quality data in discrete spaces, including text, but accelerating their sampling remains comparatively underexplored. This paper focuses on the computational work performed during generation. Its proposed discrete non-Markov diffusion models induce a set of predetermined transition times that can be used to organize the sampling process.

That structure enables a sampling algorithm requiring no additional training and substantially fewer neural-network evaluations. Each evaluation is a call to the model, so reducing their number makes sampling faster. The contribution links the formulation of the diffusion process to a concrete reduction in the repeated computation needed to generate outputs.

The authors also study how sampling changes as the number of steps moves from finite to infinite, connecting discrete-step and continuous-time descriptions of discrete diffusion. Experiments on natural-language generation and machine translation report improvements in both generation speed and sample quality compared with existing discrete diffusion methods. The findings therefore support the approach as an acceleration method that also improves output quality in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2024-fast-sampling-via-discrete-.tldr: Predetermined transition times enable training-free discrete diffusion sampling with fewer network calls and improved reported speed and sample quality.

paragraphs: Biological sequence editing seeks changes that improve a desired property while keeping the number of alterations small. Limiting edits helps preserve predictability and may support safety, making the extent of modification part of the design problem. GFNSeqEditor addresses this task using generative flow networks to produce multiple candidate edits from a starting sequence.

The algorithm first identifies elements of the seed sequence that may weaken the desired biological property. A learned stochastic policy then edits those locations, allowing different modifications to be proposed for the same starting point. Specific hyperparameters regulate the number of changes, giving the method a way to control how extensively it alters a sequence.

Experiments across real-world datasets and biological applications report better performance than existing state-of-the-art sequence-editing methods. The approach brings together targeted selection of edit locations, diversity among proposed modifications, and control over edit count. The abstract presents limited editing as potentially supportive of safety; the reported performance results establish advantages in the evaluated editing tasks rather than a general safety guarantee.
neurips-2024-gflownet-assisted-biologica.tldr: GFNSeqEditor uses a learned stochastic editing policy to propose diverse biological sequence improvements with a controllable number of changes.

paragraphs: When training data is uncertain, several different datasets may be consistent with what is known. Each possible dataset can lead to a different learned model and different predictions. This paper develops a method for linear models that follows these possibilities through training, so uncertainty in the data becomes explicit uncertainty in the resulting models.

The method uses abstract interpretation and geometric objects called zonotopes to compactly represent collections of dataset variations. It then symbolically executes gradient descent across all represented possibilities at once. The authors develop techniques that make this process converge to a fixed point and derive closed-form expressions for that fixed point.

The outputs are sound over-approximations of the possible optimal models and corresponding prediction ranges. This means the representation contains the relevant possibilities, though it can also include additional ones introduced by the approximation. Theoretical and empirical analyses demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. Its significance is a structured way to reason about how training-data quality issues propagate into model choice and prediction uncertainty.
neurips-2024-learning-from-uncertain-dat.tldr: The method symbolically trains linear models across uncertain dataset variations to bound possible models and prediction ranges.

paragraphs: Neural image compression must convert learned image features into discrete values that can be stored or transmitted. Uniform scalar quantization handles features individually and is commonly used because it is computationally manageable. Vector quantization can exploit relationships between features, but its greater complexity makes it harder to deploy.

Lattice vector quantization offers a structured alternative with computational efficiency close to scalar quantization. Its traditional structures, however, are optimized for uniformly distributed sources and may fit actual neural latent features poorly. The paper proposes learning lattice codebooks from the statistics of the features being compressed, adapting the quantization structure to their observed distribution.

The resulting optimal lattice vector quantization method targets the rate-distortion trade-off: balancing the amount of encoded data against reconstruction error. The authors report significant improvements over existing quantization schemes while retaining the practical manageability associated with uniform scalar quantization. The central contribution is making an efficient, structured quantizer responsive to the latent data it actually encounters, rather than relying on a distributional design that may be mismatched.
neurips-2024-learning-optimal-lattice-ve.tldr: Learning lattice quantization codebooks from latent-feature statistics improves the reported compression trade-off while retaining computational practicality.

paragraphs: A common image-classification workflow uses a pretrained model to extract features and trains a separate classifier on those features. Biases inherited from the pretrained model can hurt downstream performance. Addressing them becomes more difficult when the feature extractor is a black box whose weights or architecture are unavailable, or whose scale prevents updating it.

This paper studies debiasing under that restriction: the classifier can be fine-tuned, but the feature encoder cannot. The authors examine how suitable existing debiasing methods are for this setting and propose a clustering-based adaptive margin loss. Their method works with the black-box encoder and does not require knowing which attribute is responsible for the bias.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness. The contribution focuses attention on a practical distinction between changing a representation and improving a classifier that must use a fixed representation. By operating within the latter constraint and without bias-attribute knowledge, the approach addresses a setting where direct modification of the pretrained model is unavailable.
neurips-2024-mitigating-biases-in-blackb.tldr: A clustering-based adaptive margin loss helps debias downstream image classifiers when the feature extractor is fixed and the bias attribute is unknown.

paragraphs: Devices can maintain connections to multiple networks, such as Wi-Fi and cellular services, at the same time. Making useful joint use of those connections requires deciding how to distribute each device's traffic as conditions change. NetworkGym provides a high-fidelity simulation environment for training and evaluating reinforcement-learning solutions to this traffic-splitting problem.

The simulator supports multiple traffic flows and splitting across access networks. Initial evaluations find that most tested state-of-the-art offline reinforcement-learning algorithms, including CQL, do not outperform certain handcrafted heuristics on average. This result motivates broader evaluation beyond familiar benchmarks: success elsewhere does not establish that an algorithm will handle this networking task well.

The paper also introduces Pessimistic TD3, an extension of TD3+BC that uses value-function pessimism as a behavioral constraint. The mechanism has theoretical motivation and is described as relatively simple to implement. It outperforms many evaluated offline reinforcement-learning methods. Together, the simulator, offline datasets, and algorithm provide a concrete setting for studying where offline learning succeeds or struggles in network traffic management.
neurips-2024-networkgym-reinforcement-le.tldr: NetworkGym benchmarks multi-network traffic splitting and introduces a pessimistic offline learning method that outperforms many tested alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper studies how training-data choices affect cultural and socioeconomic coverage in contrastive vision-language models. Across a broad collection of datasets and evaluation measures, it finds that restricting image-text training pairs to English disadvantages lower-socioeconomic-status communities and weakens cultural understanding. The effect makes language filtering consequential for which communities a model represents well.

The authors also find that commonly used metrics based on ImageNet and COCO fail to capture this gap and can even point in the opposite direction. Consequently, favorable results on those Western-centric benchmarks can coexist with weaker performance on broader cultural coverage. The study connects the training-data issue with a separate issue in how progress is measured.

A proposed training sequence first uses global, unfiltered data and then fine-tunes on English content. The reported findings show that this can improve cultural understanding without sacrificing performance on the popular benchmarks. The paper additionally introduces geolocation as an evaluation task for cultural diversity. Together, these contributions support broader training data and evaluations that expose differences hidden by standard benchmark scores.
neurips-2024-no-filter-cultural-and-soci.tldr: English-only data filtering can weaken cultural coverage, while global pretraining can improve it without reducing performance on common benchmarks.

paragraphs: Normalization can improve neural-network training, but it also changes how parameter magnitudes interact with learning. The paper identifies an equivalence between growing parameter norms and a shrinking effective learning rate. In continual learning, this implicit reduction can happen too quickly, leaving the model with little ability to adapt over the timescale of the problem.

Normalize-and-Project combines normalization layers with weight projection to keep the effective learning rate constant throughout training. This reparameterization makes learning-rate control explicit instead of allowing parameter growth to impose an implicit schedule. It also provides an analytical tool for investigating how learning-rate schedules influence deep reinforcement learning.

The authors report improved robustness to changing conditions on synthetic benchmarks of lost learning capacity and on single-task and sequential versions of the Arcade Learning Environment. They also apply the approach to ResNets and transformers, recovering baseline performance and sometimes slightly improving it on stationary benchmarks. These results connect the method's control of effective step size with better continued adaptation, while showing compatibility with familiar network architectures.
neurips-2024-normalization-and-effective.tldr: Normalize-and-Project prevents parameter growth from implicitly shrinking effective learning rates and improves reported robustness to changing learning conditions.

paragraphs: A deployed classifier may encounter changing data distributions before new labels become available. This paper considers online label-shift adaptation under that constraint. Existing methods largely adjust the final layer of a pretrained classifier, while the authors investigate whether the feature representation itself can also be improved using the unlabeled incoming data.

Their method, OLS-OFU, uses self-supervised learning to update feature extraction at test time. These feature updates become part of the ongoing adaptation process, allowing the prediction model to benefit from a changing representation as well as adjustments to its classification stage. The approach therefore expands which parts of the model participate in responding to distribution changes.

The theoretical analysis preserves online regret convergence similar to existing results while accounting for the improved features. Empirically, the gains over existing adaptation methods are reported to be as substantial as those methods' gains over a baseline with no adaptation. The findings support online representation updates as a meaningful addition to label-shift correction, with both a theoretical treatment and evidence of practical prediction improvements.
neurips-2024-online-feature-updates-impr.tldr: OLS-OFU improves online label-shift adaptation by updating feature representations through self-supervised learning on unlabeled test data.

paragraphs: This paper addresses language models producing negative or toxic content in response to some prompts. Its focus includes harmful outcomes that occur rarely but remain significant. The proposed approach brings risk aversion into fine-tuning so that these undesirable outcomes receive explicit attention in the training objective.

The method optimizes Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR, within reinforcement learning with human feedback. CVaR directs attention toward the unfavorable part of an outcome distribution, making it relevant when occasional severe failures matter. Applied here, the objective is to reduce harmful generations while preserving the model's effectiveness on generative tasks.

The authors evaluate the approach on sentiment modification and toxicity mitigation, reporting that risk-averse training improves avoidance of toxic outputs while maintaining task effectiveness. These findings support treating the distribution of undesirable outcomes as part of the fine-tuning problem. The contribution is an objective-level approach to reducing harmful responses, with the reported empirical support coming from the two evaluated task types.
neurips-2024-risk-averse-fine-tuning-of-.tldr: Risk-averse fine-tuning uses CVaR to reduce toxic language-model outputs while preserving effectiveness in the evaluated generative tasks.

paragraphs: Neural image compressors encode an image into a quantized latent representation that a decoder turns back into an image. Even successful pretrained models can produce suboptimal representations because optimization is imperfect and encoder and decoder capacity is limited. Refining the latent representation provides another opportunity to improve the balance between encoded size and reconstruction quality.

The paper introduces SGA+, a collection of three methods extending stochastic Gumbel annealing for latent refinement. The approach builds on using an existing compression model and improving its latents. The authors evaluate it with a pretrained hyperprior model and a more flexible model, examining how refinement changes the rate-distortion trade-off.

The proposed methods improve compression performance over their predecessors, and the best-performing method produces gains on Tecnick and CLIC. A detailed analysis also finds lower sensitivity to hyperparameter choices. Finally, each method is extended from two-class to three-class rounding. Together, these results support latent refinement as a useful source of compression improvements, with greater robustness to configuration choices in the reported analysis.
neurips-2024-robustly-overfitting-latent.tldr: SGA+ refines pretrained image-compression latents to improve rate-distortion performance with reduced sensitivity to hyperparameter choices.

paragraphs: Some machine-learning systems take neural networks themselves as inputs. Designing these systems requires accounting for different parameter arrangements that represent equivalent computations. Prior designs emphasize neuron permutations, but this paper examines additional scaling symmetries associated with activation functions such as ReLU, sine, and tanh.

ScaleGMNs adapt graph metanetworks to respect valid multiplications and divisions of weights and biases. Their neuron and edge representations transform consistently under these scalings. New building blocks support either corresponding transformations or unchanged outputs under individual scalar factors and their products, incorporating the symmetry throughout the message-passing framework.

Under stated expressivity conditions, the authors prove that ScaleGMN can simulate the forward and backward passes of any input feedforward neural network. Experiments also report state-of-the-art improvements across several datasets and activation functions. The theoretical result depends on those expressivity conditions, while the empirical results support scaling symmetry as a useful architectural bias. The contribution broadens the transformations that network-processing models explicitly recognize beyond neuron reordering.
neurips-2024-scale-equivariant-graph-met.tldr: ScaleGMNs incorporate valid parameter-scaling symmetries into graph models that process neural networks, improving reported performance across several settings.

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps client data local while sharing gradient updates with a server. Those updates can nevertheless reveal the data that produced them. SPEAR studies this exposure in the honest-but-curious setting, where the server follows the protocol but examines the information it receives. Earlier attacks in this setting achieved exact reconstruction only for single-example batches.

SPEAR combines the low-rank structure of gradients with a sampling-based algorithm to reconstruct entire batches exactly. A central step uses sparsity caused by ReLU activations to reject many incorrect samples. This filtering makes the final reconstruction computationally tractable, connecting a structural property of the network to the attack's practical feasibility.

The GPU implementation targets fully connected networks and exactly recovers high-dimensional ImageNet inputs in batches of up to approximately 25 examples while scaling to large networks. Separately, the authors prove that much larger batches can be reconstructed with high probability given exponential time. The distinction matters: the practical implementation and the larger-batch theoretical result establish different levels of computational feasibility.
neurips-2024-spear-exact-gradient-invers.tldr: SPEAR exactly reconstructs multi-example batches from shared gradients, demonstrating a privacy exposure in the studied federated-learning setting.

paragraphs: Evaluating street-scene surface reconstruction requires reliable reference geometry. Existing driving datasets provide noisy LiDAR points, which can be insufficient for judging precise surface positions and do not provide the surface-normal information needed to evaluate orientation. SS3DM addresses this evaluation problem by supplying synthetic street scenes with precise 3D mesh references.

The meshes are exported from the CARLA simulator and include both surface locations and normal vectors. Normal vectors describe which direction a surface faces, adding a geometric property beyond position alone. To generate reconstruction inputs resembling driving observations, the authors virtually drive a vehicle equipped with six RGB cameras and five LiDAR sensors through diverse outdoor scenes.

The dataset supports a benchmark of state-of-the-art surface-reconstruction methods and an evaluation of the challenges they face. Its contribution is the combination of simulated sensor observations and detailed reference surfaces against which reconstructions can be checked. This makes position and orientation assessment possible within the synthetic setting, strengthening evaluation for applications such as autonomous-driving simulation and digital entertainment.
neurips-2024-ss3dm-benchmarking-street-v.tldr: SS3DM supplies precise synthetic street-scene meshes and sensor observations for evaluating reconstructed surface positions and orientations.

paragraphs: This paper studies in-context learning through statistical learning theory: how a pretrained transformer can use examples in its input to learn a new regression task. The analyzed architecture combines a deep neural network with one linear attention layer. Its pretraining tasks come from broad nonparametric function classes, including Besov spaces and piecewise smooth functions.

The analysis shows that sufficiently trained transformers can attain, and under the studied setup even improve upon, the minimax estimation-risk benchmark by learning relevant basis representations during pretraining. Minimax risk describes performance against the hardest cases in a specified function class. Learned representations are therefore central to the result, connecting previous task experience with efficient learning from context.

The authors separately analyze generalization during pretraining and during in-context learning. They establish upper and lower bounds involving both the number of pretraining tasks and the number of examples in context, with extensions to high-dimensional or sequential data. These conditional theoretical findings help explain the roles of task diversity and representation learning in few-shot prompting for the model and task families studied.
neurips-2024-transformers-are-minimax-op.tldr: For a specified transformer and regression-task setup, learned representations enable sufficiently trained models to reach strong theoretical in-context estimation guarantees.

paragraphs: Understanding responses to visual content involves both where people look and how they judge what they see. Earlier work often treats these early perceptual behaviors and later subjective responses separately, sometimes within a single content category. UniAR brings attention and preference prediction together in one model across several types of visual material.

The model uses a multimodal transformer to predict subjective feedback, including satisfaction or aesthetic quality, alongside attention or interaction heatmaps and viewing order. These outputs cover both overall judgments and the spatial and sequential patterns associated with viewing. Training draws on public datasets of natural images, webpages, and graphic designs.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks spanning different image domains and behavior-modeling tasks. The results support a unified approach to predicting these related aspects of human response. Potential uses include rapid feedback on interface or visual-content effectiveness and guidance for designers or content-generation models. These are presented as possible applications of the predictive capabilities, rather than established outcomes for every design workflow.
neurips-2024-uniar-a-unified-model-for-p.tldr: UniAR jointly predicts attention patterns, viewing order, and subjective responses across natural images, webpages, and graphic designs.

paragraphs: Large visual datasets can contain recurring associations that models learn even when those associations are unreliable for prediction. ConBias examines this problem through concept co-occurrence: which concepts appear together and how unevenly those combinations are represented. The framework aims both to diagnose these patterns across a dataset and to reduce their effect on downstream learning.

ConBias represents the dataset as a knowledge graph of concepts, making relationships among concepts available for analysis. It uses this graph to identify spurious co-occurrences and imbalances. A clique-based balancing strategy then addresses those imbalances by considering groups of mutually connected concepts, connecting the diagnostic representation with a method for modifying the training distribution.

The authors report that data augmentation guided by the balanced concept distribution improves generalization across multiple datasets compared with state-of-the-art methods. The findings support examining combinations of concepts when curating visual data. The contribution combines a way to inspect dataset-wide associations with a balancing procedure whose usefulness is evaluated through the performance of models trained on the augmented data.
neurips-2024-visual-data-diagnosis-and-d.tldr: ConBias uses concept graphs to diagnose co-occurrence imbalances and guide data augmentation that improves reported generalization.

paragraphs: Understanding animal social interaction requires identifying who produces acoustic signals, alongside other behavioral and neural observations. Sound-source localization offers a way to locate these signals, but existing approaches have limitations in standard laboratory environments. The VCL Benchmark provides a shared resource for evaluating localization algorithms specifically on rodent vocalizations.

The dataset contains synchronized video and multichannel audio for 767,295 sounds with annotated source locations across nine conditions. Those source annotations provide references against which an algorithm's estimated locations can be assessed. The benchmark includes evaluations using real recordings, simulated acoustic data, and combinations of the two, bringing several data settings into one evaluation resource.

The paper presents VCL as the first large-scale benchmark dataset for rodent sound-source localization and addresses a lack of public resources for systematic evaluation in bioacoustics. Its main contribution is infrastructure for comparing methods, rather than a reported claim that one localization algorithm solves the problem. The intended benefit is to connect acoustic machine-learning research with neuroscience experiments that need reliable attribution of social vocalizations.
neurips-2024-vocal-call-locator-benchmar.tldr: VCL provides annotated rodent audio and synchronized video to benchmark sound-source localization on real and simulated data.
